questions.q: Which layer of the superficial fascia of the lower anterior abdominal wall is membranous and continuous inferiorly with Colles fascia of the perineum?
questions.explain: Scarpa fascia is the deep membranous layer of the superficial abdominal fascia that continues inferiorly into the perineum as superficial perineal (Colles) fascia and fuses with the fascia lata just below the inguinal ligament. Camper fascia is the superficial fatty layer.

open.q: Name the deep membranous layer of the superficial fascia of the lower anterior abdominal wall that is continuous inferiorly with Colles fascia of the perineum.
accept: deep layer of superficial abdominal fascia

questions.q: The arcuate line (semicircular line of Douglas) on the posterior wall of the rectus sheath is located approximately midway between the umbilicus and which bony landmark?
questions.explain: The arcuate line marks the inferior limit of the posterior layer of the rectus sheath, situated roughly halfway between the umbilicus and the pubic symphysis.

open.q: The arcuate line of the rectus sheath lies approximately midway between the umbilicus and which anterior pelvic landmark?

questions.q: Which structure enters the rectus sheath at the arcuate line to ascend on the posterior surface of the rectus abdominis muscle?
questions.explain: The inferior epigastric artery, a branch of the external iliac artery, pierces the transversalis fascia and enters the rectus sheath by passing anterior to the arcuate line. The superior epigastric artery enters superiorly between the sternal and costal slips of the diaphragm.

open.q: Which artery enters the rectus sheath by passing anterior to the arcuate line to ascend behind the rectus abdominis?

questions.q: The anterior wall of the inguinal canal is formed primarily by the aponeurosis of which muscle?
questions.explain: The external oblique aponeurosis forms the entire anterior wall of the inguinal canal, reinforced laterally by the lowest fibers of the internal oblique muscle.

open.q: Which abdominal muscle's aponeurosis forms the primary anterior wall of the inguinal canal?

questions.q: The deep inguinal ring is an oval opening located in which fascial layer?
questions.explain: The deep inguinal ring is an evagination of the transversalis fascia located just lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels and midway between the anterior superior iliac spine and the pubic symphysis. The superficial inguinal ring is a defect in the external oblique aponeurosis.

open.q: In which fascial layer is the deep inguinal ring located?

questions.q: Which nerve traverses the inguinal canal and emerges through the superficial inguinal ring without passing through the deep inguinal ring?
questions.explain: The ilioinguinal nerve (L1) pierces the internal oblique muscle to enter the inguinal canal from its lateral wall and exits via the superficial inguinal ring to supply the skin of the upper medial thigh and anterior scrotum or labium majus.

open.q: Name the branch of the lumbar plexus (L1) that enters the inguinal canal through the internal oblique muscle and exits via the superficial inguinal ring.

questions.q: A 55-year-old man develops a reducible bulge in the groin that protrudes through Hesselbach triangle medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. Which type of hernia does he have?
questions.explain: Direct inguinal hernias are acquired weaknesses in the posterior wall of the inguinal canal within Hesselbach (inguinal) triangle, lying medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. Indirect inguinal hernias enter the deep inguinal ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels.

open.q: What type of inguinal hernia protrudes directly through Hesselbach triangle medial to the inferior epigastric vessels?

questions.q: Which structure forms the lateral border of Hesselbach (inguinal) triangle?
questions.explain: Hesselbach triangle is bounded laterally by the inferior epigastric vessels, medially by the lateral margin of the rectus abdominis muscle (linea semilunaris), and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament.

open.q: Which blood vessels form the lateral boundary of Hesselbach (inguinal) triangle?

questions.q: The umbilical preperitoneal fold (median umbilical fold) covers which embryological remnant?
questions.explain: The median umbilical fold covers the median umbilical ligament, which is the fibrous remnant of the urachus (allantois). The medial umbilical folds cover the obliterated umbilical arteries, and the lateral umbilical folds cover the inferior epigastric vessels.

open.q: Which embryological remnant is covered by the median umbilical fold on the deep surface of the anterior abdominal wall?

questions.q: From which layer of the anterior abdominal wall is the cremasteric muscle and fascia derived?
questions.explain: As the testis and spermatic cord descend through the inguinal canal, the internal oblique contributes the cremasteric muscle and fascia. The external oblique forms the external spermatic fascia, and the transversalis fascia forms the internal spermatic fascia.

open.q: Which anterior abdominal wall muscle gives rise to the cremasteric muscle and fascia of the spermatic cord?

questions.q: Which abdominal dermatome corresponds to the level of the umbilicus?
questions.explain: The skin around the umbilicus is innervated by the anterior cutaneous branch of the T10 spinal nerve. T7 supplies the epigastrium near the xiphoid process, and L1 supplies the suprapubic and inguinal regions.

open.q: Which thoracic spinal nerve dermatome supplies the skin at the level of the umbilicus?

questions.q: In portal hypertension, dilated superficial veins radiating from the umbilicus (caput medusae) result from portosystemic anastomosis between the paraumbilical veins and which systemic veins?
questions.explain: Paraumbilical veins running in the falciform ligament connect the left branch of the portal vein to the superficial epigastric, thoracoepigastric, and inferior epigastric systemic veins around the umbilicus.

open.q: With which systemic veins do the paraumbilical veins anastomose around the umbilicus to produce caput medusae in portal hypertension?

questions.q: Which structure forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow)?
questions.explain: The epiploic foramen is bounded anteriorly by the free edge of the lesser omentum (hepatoduodenal ligament) containing the portal triad, posteriorly by the inferior vena cava, superiorly by the caudate lobe of the liver, and inferiorly by the first part of the duodenum.

open.q: Which peritoneal ligament forms the anterior boundary of the epiploic foramen (foramen of Winslow)?

questions.q: Which of the following abdominal organs is classified as secondarily retroperitoneal?
questions.explain: The ascending and descending colon, most of the duodenum, and the pancreas (except the tail) develop with a mesentery and later fuse with the posterior abdominal wall, becoming secondarily retroperitoneal. The spleen, transverse colon, and jejunum remain intraperitoneal.

open.q: Between the ascending colon and transverse colon, which segment is secondarily retroperitoneal?

questions.q: The root of the mesentery of the small intestine extends obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure to which structure?
questions.explain: The root of the mesentery is about 15 cm long and runs obliquely from the duodenojejunal flexure on the left of L2 down and to the right to the ileocecal junction in the right iliac fossa.

open.q: Where does the root of the mesentery of the small intestine terminate inferiorly and to the right?

questions.q: In a supine patient, fluid in the peritoneal cavity tends to gravitate first into which recess of the supracolic compartment?
questions.explain: In the supine position, the hepatorenal recess (pouch of Morison) between the visceral surface of the right lobe of the liver and the right kidney is the lowest point of the supracolic peritoneal cavity, making it a prime site for fluid accumulation on ultrasound (FAST scan).

open.q: Name the peritoneal recess between the right lobe of the liver and the right kidney that forms the lowest point of the upper abdomen in a supine patient.

questions.q: Which blood vessels run within the gastrosplenic ligament?
options: Short gastric and left gastro-omental vessels
Right gastric and proper hepatic vessels
questions.explain: The gastrosplenic ligament connects the greater curvature of the stomach to the hilum of the spleen and transmits the short gastric and left gastro-omental (gastroepiploic) vessels. The splenic artery and vein travel in the splenorenal ligament.

open.q: Which arteries travel within the gastrosplenic ligament from the splenic artery to the greater curvature of the stomach?
accept: short gastric arteries and left gastro-omental artery
short gastric and left gastroepiploic vessels

questions.q: During a Pringle maneuver to control severe hepatic bleeding, a surgeon compresses the hepatoduodenal ligament between thumb and index finger. Which structure is NOT compressed in this maneuver?
questions.explain: The hepatoduodenal ligament encloses the portal triad (hepatic artery proper, hepatic portal vein, and common bile duct). The inferior vena cava lies posterior to the epiploic foramen and is not compressed.

open.q: List the three structures enclosed within the hepatoduodenal ligament that are compressed during the Pringle maneuver.
accept: hepatic artery proper, portal vein, and common bile duct
hepatic artery, portal vein, bile duct

questions.q: Which artery supplies the lesser curvature of the stomach directly from the celiac trunk?
questions.explain: The left gastric artery arises directly from the celiac trunk, ascends to the esophagogastric junction, and runs along the lesser curvature to anastomose with the right gastric artery (a branch of the hepatic artery proper).

open.q: Which branch of the celiac trunk runs directly along the lesser curvature of the stomach?

questions.q: A penetrating posterior gastric ulcer erodes through the posterior wall of the stomach into the omental bursa. Which large artery lying immediately on the pancreas in the stomach bed is at greatest risk of catastrophic hemorrhage?
questions.explain: The tortuous splenic artery runs along the superior border of the pancreas directly posterior to the stomach (forming part of the stomach bed) and is classically eroded by posterior gastric ulcers.

open.q: Which large artery running along the superior border of the pancreas in the stomach bed is most vulnerable to erosion by a posterior gastric ulcer?

questions.q: Which part of the duodenum is completely intraperitoneal and commonly affected by duodenal ulcers?
questions.explain: The proximal 2 to 3 cm of the first part of the duodenum (duodenal bulb or cap) is intraperitoneal, suspended by the hepatoduodenal ligament. The remainder of the duodenum is retroperitoneal.

open.q: Which part of the duodenum has an intraperitoneal proximal segment known clinically as the duodenal cap?

questions.q: A perforated ulcer on the posterior wall of the first part of the duodenum most frequently causes severe bleeding from which artery?
questions.explain: The gastroduodenal artery descends directly posterior to the first part of the duodenum before dividing into the right gastro-omental and superior pancreaticoduodenal arteries, making it vulnerable to posterior duodenal ulcers.

open.q: Which artery descends immediately posterior to the first part of the duodenum and is commonly eroded by posterior duodenal ulcers?

questions.q: On which wall of the second (descending) part of the duodenum does the major duodenal papilla open?
questions.explain: The hepatopancreatic ampulla (of Vater) opens onto the summit of the major duodenal papilla on the posteromedial wall of the descending (second) part of the duodenum.

open.q: On which wall of the descending part of the duodenum is the major duodenal papilla situated?

questions.q: The third (horizontal) part of the duodenum crosses the midline at the level of L3 and can become compressed in the angle between the abdominal aorta and which anterior vessel?
questions.explain: The third part of the duodenum and the left renal vein pass through the narrow angle between the abdominal aorta posteriorly and the superior mesenteric artery anteriorly, which can cause superior mesenteric artery syndrome or nutcracker syndrome.

open.q: Which major artery crosses anteriorly over the third part of the duodenum and the left renal vein?

questions.q: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) attaches the duodenojejunal flexure to which structure?
questions.explain: The suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) arises from the right crus of the diaphragm around the esophageal hiatus and inserts onto the duodenojejunal flexure, serving as the anatomical landmark separating upper from lower gastrointestinal bleeding.

open.q: From which diaphragmatic structure does the suspensory muscle of the duodenum (ligament of Treitz) originate?

questions.q: Which anatomical feature distinguishes the jejunum from the ileum?
options: Longer vasa recta and fewer arterial arcades
Greater mesenteric fat extending to the bowel wall
questions.explain: The jejunum has a wider diameter, thicker wall, prominent plicae circulares, less mesenteric fat, fewer arterial arcades (1 to 2), and longer vasa recta compared to the ileum.

open.q: Compare the vasa recta and arterial arcades of the jejunum with those of the ileum.
accept: jejunum has longer vasa recta and fewer arcades
longer vasa recta, fewer arterial arcades

questions.q: Meckel diverticulum is a congenital remnant of the omphalomesenteric (vitelline) duct typically located on the antimesenteric border of the ileum within how many feet of the ileocecal valve?
questions.explain: Meckel diverticulum follows the rule of 2s: occurs in about 2% of the population, is roughly 2 inches long, lies within 2 feet (60 cm) proximal to the ileocecal valve, and is twice as common in males.

open.q: Within approximately how many feet proximal to the ileocecal valve is a Meckel diverticulum typically located?

questions.q: Which of the following is a cardinal macroscopic feature that distinguishes the colon from the small intestine?
questions.explain: The colon is characterized by teniae coli (three longitudinal smooth muscle bands), haustra (sacculations), and omental appendices (appendices epiploicae). Plicae circulares, villi, and Peyer patches are features of the small intestine.

open.q: Name the three longitudinal bands of smooth muscle on the outer wall of the colon that converge at the base of the appendix.

questions.q: Which artery supplies the vermiform appendix and runs in the free edge of the mesoappendix?
questions.explain: The appendicular artery is an end-artery arising from the ileocolic artery (the terminal branch of the superior mesenteric artery) and travels within the mesoappendix.

open.q: From which branch of the superior mesenteric artery does the appendicular artery arise?

questions.q: Early pain in acute appendicitis is typically felt as a dull ache in the periumbilical region before localizing to McBurney point. Which spinal cord segments mediate this early referred visceral pain?
questions.explain: Visceral afferent pain fibers from the appendix travel with sympathetic fibers via the lesser splanchnic nerve to the T10 spinal cord segment, which also receives somatic sensation from the periumbilical dermatome (T10). Once the inflamed appendix irritates parietal peritoneum, somatic pain localizes to the right iliac fossa.

open.q: Which spinal cord segment mediates the initial periumbilical referred pain of acute appendicitis?

questions.q: The marginal artery of Drummond provides critical collateral circulation along the colon by anastomosing branches of the superior mesenteric artery with which artery?
questions.explain: The marginal artery of Drummond runs along the mesenteric border of the colon, connecting the ileocolic, right colic, and middle colic branches of the superior mesenteric artery with the left colic and sigmoid branches of the inferior mesenteric artery.

open.q: Which two major unpaired abdominal aortic branches are linked along the colon by the marginal artery of Drummond?

questions.q: Which region of the colon represents the classic watershed area (Griffiths point) most susceptible to ischemia during systemic hypotension?
questions.explain: The splenic (left colic) flexure is a watershed zone between the middle colic artery (SMA) and left colic artery (IMA) where the marginal artery is often weak or incomplete, making it prone to ischemic colitis.

open.q: Which flexure of the colon is a vascular watershed area between the superior and inferior mesenteric arteries?

questions.sub: Liver, Biliary Tract, Pancreas, and Spleen
questions.q: The falciform ligament divides the liver anatomically into right and left lobes and contains which structure in its free inferior margin?
questions.explain: The ligamentum teres hepatis (round ligament of the liver), the obliterated remnant of the left umbilical vein, runs in the free edge of the falciform ligament.

open.q: Which fibrous remnant of the left umbilical vein runs in the free inferior edge of the falciform ligament?

questions.sub: Liver, Biliary Tract, Pancreas, and Spleen
questions.q: The functional (surgical) division of the liver into right and left hemilivers is defined by Cantlie line, which extends from the gallbladder fossa to which posterior structure?
questions.explain: Cantlie line runs along the plane of the middle hepatic vein from the fundus of the gallbladder fossa anteriorly to the sulcus for the inferior vena cava posteriorly, dividing the liver into functional right and left halves based on portal triad supply.

open.q: Cantlie line separates the functional right and left lobes of the liver by extending from the gallbladder fossa to which major vein?

questions.sub: Liver, Biliary Tract, Pancreas, and Spleen
questions.q: Which functional hepatic segment (Couinaud Segment I) receives portal blood from both right and left portal branches and drains directly into the inferior vena cava via independent emissary veins?
questions.explain: The caudate lobe (Segment I) has independent blood supply from both right and left branches of the portal vein and hepatic artery, and its hepatic veins drain directly into the IVC—allowing it to hypertrophy in Budd-Chiari syndrome.

open.q: Which lobe of the liver corresponds to Couinaud Segment I and drains directly into the inferior vena cava?

questions.sub: Liver, Biliary Tract, Pancreas, and Spleen
questions.q: What are the three boundaries of the cystohepatic triangle (triangle of Calot)?
options: Common hepatic duct, cystic duct, and inferior surface of the liver
Common bile duct, portal vein, and hepatic artery proper
Right hepatic duct, left hepatic duct, and falciform ligament
questions.explain: The cystohepatic triangle is bounded medially by the common hepatic duct, inferiorly by the cystic duct, and superiorly by the visceral (inferior) surface of the liver. It typically contains the cystic artery.

open.q: Name the three anatomical boundaries of the cystohepatic triangle (triangle of Calot).
accept: common hepatic duct, cystic duct, and inferior surface of liver
common hepatic duct, cystic duct, liver edge

questions.sub: Liver, Biliary Tract, Pancreas, and Spleen
questions.q: From which artery does the cystic artery most commonly arise?
questions.explain: In roughly 75% of individuals, the cystic artery arises from the right hepatic artery within the cystohepatic triangle.

open.q: Which branch of the hepatic artery proper most commonly gives rise to the cystic artery?

questions.sub: Liver, Biliary Tract, Pancreas, and Spleen
questions.q: A 48-year-old woman with acute cholecystitis presents with pain radiating to the tip of her right shoulder. Irritation of the diaphragmatic peritoneum by the inflamed gallbladder is transmitted by which nerve?
questions.explain: Inflammation of the gallbladder can irritate the overlying diaphragmatic peritoneum supplied by the right phrenic nerve (C3-C5), referring somatic pain to the C3-C5 dermatomes over the right shoulder tip (Kehr sign).

open.q: Which nerve transmits diaphragmatic peritoneal irritation from an inflamed gallbladder to produce referred right shoulder-tip pain?

questions.sub: Liver, Biliary Tract, Pancreas, and Spleen
questions.q: Which vascular landmark lies immediately posterior to the neck of the pancreas?
options: Formation of the hepatic portal vein
questions.explain: The splenic vein and superior mesenteric vein unite directly posterior to the neck of the pancreas (at the L1-L2 level) to form the hepatic portal vein.

open.q: Which major vein is formed immediately posterior to the neck of the pancreas by the union of the splenic and superior mesenteric veins?

questions.sub: Liver, Biliary Tract, Pancreas, and Spleen
questions.q: The uncinate process of the pancreas projects medially behind the superior mesenteric vessels and lies anterior to which vessel?
questions.explain: The uncinate process hooks behind the superior mesenteric artery and vein and rests directly anterior to the abdominal aorta.

open.q: Which part of the pancreas hooks posteriorly behind the superior mesenteric vessels?

questions.sub: Liver, Biliary Tract, Pancreas, and Spleen
questions.q: Against which ribs does the long axis of the spleen lie in the left hypochondrium?
questions.explain: The spleen lies beneath the left 9th, 10th, and 11th ribs, with its long axis parallel to the 10th rib, separated from the ribs by the diaphragm and left costodiaphragmatic recess.

open.q: Which three ribs overlie the spleen on the left posterolateral thoracic wall?

questions.sub: Liver, Biliary Tract, Pancreas, and Spleen
questions.q: During a splenectomy, clamping the splenorenal ligament too deeply risks injuring which structure whose tip extends into the hilum of the spleen?
questions.explain: The tail of the pancreas is the only intraperitoneal part of the pancreas; it travels within the splenorenal (lienorenal) ligament to reach the splenic hilum and can be inadvertently damaged during splenectomy.

open.q: Which portion of the pancreas lies within the splenorenal ligament and is vulnerable to injury during splenectomy?

questions.q: At the lower end of the esophagus, the esophageal branches of the left gastric vein anastomose with esophageal tributaries of which systemic venous system?
questions.explain: Submucosal esophageal veins draining into the left gastric vein (portal) anastomose with esophageal veins draining into the azygos and hemiazygos veins (systemic), leading to esophageal varices in portal hypertension.

open.q: With which systemic venous system do the esophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein anastomose at the gastroesophageal junction?

questions.q: In the anal canal, portosystemic anastomosis occurs between the superior rectal vein (portal) and which systemic veins?
questions.explain: The superior rectal vein drains into the inferior mesenteric vein (portal), whereas the middle and inferior rectal veins drain into the internal iliac and internal pudendal veins (systemic).

open.q: Name the two systemic veins that anastomose with the superior rectal vein in the wall of the anal canal.
accept: middle rectal and inferior rectal veins

questions.q: From superficial to deep, what is the correct order of the coverings surrounding the kidney?
options: Pararenal fat, renal fascia, perirenal fat, fibrous capsule
Perirenal fat, renal fascia, pararenal fat, fibrous capsule
Renal fascia, pararenal fat, fibrous capsule, perirenal fat
Fibrous capsule, renal fascia, perirenal fat, pararenal fat
questions.explain: Moving from outside inward toward the renal parenchyma: pararenal (paranephric) fat lies outside the renal fascia (Gerota fascia), which encloses the perirenal (perinephric) fat, which in turn surrounds the true fibrous capsule of the kidney.

open.q: List the four coverings of the kidney in order from outermost (superficial) to innermost (deep).
accept: pararenal fat, renal fascia, perirenal fat, fibrous capsule
paranephric fat, Gerota fascia, perinephric fat, renal capsule

questions.q: At the hilum of the kidney, what is the standard anteroposterior arrangement of the major structures?
options: Renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis
Renal artery, renal vein, renal pelvis
Renal pelvis, renal artery, renal vein
Renal vein, renal pelvis, renal artery
questions.explain: From anterior to posterior at the renal hilum, the structures are arranged as Vein, Artery, Pelvis (mnemonic: VAP).

open.q: State the arrangement of the renal vein, renal artery, and renal pelvis from anterior to posterior at the renal hilum.

questions.q: Why do surgeons typically prefer the left kidney over the right kidney for living-donor renal transplantation?
options: The left renal vein is longer than the right renal vein
The left renal artery is shorter than the right renal artery
The left kidney has no suprarenal gland attached
The left kidney sits lower than the right kidney
questions.explain: Because the inferior vena cava lies to the right of the midline, the left renal vein must cross the abdominal aorta to reach it, making the left renal vein roughly three times longer and easier to anastomose during transplantation.

open.q: Which anatomical difference between the left and right renal vessels makes the left kidney preferred for living-donor transplantation?
accept: the left renal vein is longer

questions.q: Which three veins drain directly into the left renal vein rather than the inferior vena cava?
options: Left gonadal, left suprarenal, and left inferior phrenic veins
Right gonadal, right suprarenal, and hepatic veins
Left colic, splenic, and inferior mesenteric veins
Azygos, right renal, and lumbar veins
questions.explain: On the left side, the left gonadal (testicular/ovarian), left suprarenal, and left inferior phrenic veins drain into the left renal vein. On the right side, they drain directly into the inferior vena cava.

open.q: Name the three tributaries that drain into the left renal vein on the left side but directly into the inferior vena cava on the right side.
accept: left gonadal, left suprarenal, and left inferior phrenic veins
gonadal, suprarenal, and inferior phrenic veins

questions.q: A 24-year-old man presents with an acute left-sided varicocele that fails to empty when he lies supine. Obstruction of which vein must be suspected first, such as from a left renal cell carcinoma?
questions.explain: The left testicular vein drains at a 90-degree angle into the left renal vein. A tumor thrombus in the left renal vein (e.g., from renal cell carcinoma) obstructs left testicular venous outflow, causing a non-decompressible left varicocele.

open.q: Obstruction of which vein by a left renal cell carcinoma can present with an acute, non-decompressible left varicocele?

questions.q: Which of the following is one of the three normal anatomical constrictions of the ureter where renal calculi commonly lodge?
options: At the pelvic brim where it crosses the common iliac bifurcation
At the midpoint of the psoas major belly
questions.explain: The three physiological constrictions of the ureter are: (1) the pelviureteric junction, (2) the pelvic brim where it crosses the bifurcation of the common iliac artery (or external iliac artery), and (3) the vesicoureteric junction as it passes obliquely through the bladder wall.

open.q: Identify the three normal anatomical sites of narrowing along the course of the ureter.
accept: pelviureteric junction, pelvic brim, and vesicoureteric junction

questions.q: In the abdomen, the ureter descends vertically on the anterior surface of which muscle?
questions.explain: The abdominal ureter descends inferiorly on the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle, deep to the peritoneum, and is crossed anteriorly by the gonadal vessels.

open.q: On the anterior surface of which posterior abdominal wall muscle does the ureter descend?

questions.q: From which three arteries does each suprarenal gland receive its arterial supply?
options: Inferior phrenic artery, abdominal aorta, and renal artery
Celiac trunk, superior mesenteric artery, and renal artery
Superior mesenteric artery, lumbar artery, and gonadal artery
Splenic artery, hepatic artery, and aorta
questions.explain: Each suprarenal gland receives superior suprarenal arteries from the inferior phrenic artery, a middle suprarenal artery directly from the abdominal aorta, and an inferior suprarenal artery from the renal artery.

open.q: Name the three parent vessels that give rise to the superior, middle, and inferior suprarenal arteries.
accept: inferior phrenic artery, abdominal aorta, and renal artery

questions.q: At which vertebral level does the inferior vena cava pass through the diaphragm?
questions.explain: The caval opening in the central tendon of the diaphragm lies at the T8 vertebral level (transmitting the IVC and right phrenic nerve). The esophageal hiatus is at T10, and the aortic hiatus is at T12.

open.q: At which thoracic vertebral level does the caval opening pierce the central tendon of the diaphragm?

questions.q: Which structures pass through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at the T12 vertebral level?
options: Abdominal aorta, thoracic duct, and azygos vein
Abdominal aorta, vagal trunks, and esophageal vessels
Abdominal aorta, right phrenic nerve, and sympathetic trunks
Abdominal aorta, inferior vena cava, and cisterna chyli
questions.explain: The aortic hiatus lies behind the median arcuate ligament at T12 and transmits the abdominal aorta, the thoracic duct, and often the azygos and hemiazygos veins.

open.q: Besides the abdominal aorta, name two other structures that pass through the aortic hiatus of the diaphragm at T12.

questions.q: The medial arcuate ligament of the diaphragm is a thickening of the fascia covering which muscle?
questions.explain: The medial arcuate ligament arches over the psoas major muscle (extending from the body of L1/L2 to the transverse process of L1), whereas the lateral arcuate ligament arches over the quadratus lumborum muscle.

open.q: Over which posterior abdominal wall muscle does the medial arcuate ligament of the diaphragm arch?

questions.q: At which vertebral level does the celiac trunk arise from the anterior aspect of the abdominal aorta?
questions.explain: The celiac trunk arises just below the aortic hiatus at the T12/L1 border (T12), the superior mesenteric artery at L1, the renal arteries at L1-L2, the inferior mesenteric artery at L3, and the aortic bifurcation at L4.

open.q: At which vertebral level does the celiac trunk branch off the abdominal aorta?

questions.q: At which vertebral level does the abdominal aorta bifurcate into the right and left common iliac arteries?
questions.explain: The abdominal aorta bifurcates into the right and left common iliac arteries at the lower border of the L4 vertebra, just to the left of the midline (corresponding roughly to the supracristal plane).

open.q: At which lumbar vertebral level does the abdominal aorta divide into the left and right common iliac arteries?

questions.q: Which nerve of the lumbar plexus emerges on the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle and divides into genital and femoral branches?
questions.explain: The genitofemoral nerve (L1, L2) pierces the anterior surface of the psoas major and descends on it, dividing into the genital branch (entering the deep inguinal ring) and femoral branch (entering the femoral sheath).

open.q: Which nerve of the lumbar plexus pierces and descends along the anterior surface of the psoas major muscle?

questions.q: Which nerve of the lumbar plexus emerges along the medial border of the psoas major muscle to enter the lesser pelvis?
questions.explain: The obturator nerve (L2-L4) is the only branch of the lumbar plexus that emerges from the medial border of the psoas major; the femoral, lateral femoral cutaneous, ilioinguinal, and iliohypogastric nerves emerge along its lateral border.

open.q: Which nerve is the sole branch of the lumbar plexus to emerge from the medial border of the psoas major muscle?

questions.q: The cisterna chyli, which gives rise to the thoracic duct, is typically situated anterior to the bodies of L1 and L2 and immediately to the right of which structure?
questions.explain: The cisterna chyli lies retroperitoneally on the bodies of L1 and L2, immediately to the right of the abdominal aorta and behind the right crus of the diaphragm.

open.q: To which side of the abdominal aorta is the cisterna chyli situated at the L1-L2 vertebral level?

questions.q: Which of the following is the shortest anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic inlet and determines whether the fetal head can pass through the pelvic brim?
questions.explain: The obstetric conjugate extends from the sacral promontory to the closest point on the posterior surface of the pubic symphysis (typically about 10.5 to 11 cm). It is shorter than the anatomical conjugate and cannot be measured directly on vaginal examination.

open.q: Which anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic inlet extends from the sacral promontory to the nearest point on the posterior surface of the pubic symphysis?

questions.q: How is the obstetric conjugate clinically estimated during a bimanual pelvic examination?
options: Subtracting 1.5 to 2 cm from the diagonal conjugate
Adding 1.5 cm to the true conjugate
Measuring the distance between the ischial tuberosities
questions.explain: The diagonal conjugate (from the inferior border of the pubic symphysis to the sacral promontory) is the only anteroposterior inlet diameter measurable per vaginam; subtracting 1.5 to 2 cm estimates the obstetric conjugate.

open.q: How do you calculate the approximate obstetric conjugate from the clinically measured diagonal conjugate?

questions.q: Which diameter represents the narrowest transverse dimension of the pelvic cavity and the birth canal?
options: Transverse diameter of the pelvic inlet
questions.explain: The interspinous diameter between the left and right ischial spines (about 10 cm) is the narrowest part of the midpelvis/pelvic canal and serves as the zero station landmark for fetal head descent.

open.q: Between which two bony landmarks is the narrowest transverse diameter of the pelvic canal measured?

questions.q: Which ligament converts the greater sciatic notch into the greater sciatic foramen?
questions.explain: The sacrospinous ligament (attaching the lateral sacrum/coccyx to the ischial spine) and sacrotuberous ligament (attaching to the ischial tuberosity) convert the greater and lesser sciatic notches into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina.

open.q: Which ligament attaches to the ischial spine and divides the sciatic region into the greater and lesser sciatic foramina?

questions.q: Which muscle passes out of the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and divides it into suprapiriform and infrapiriform compartments?
questions.explain: The piriformis muscle originates from the anterior surface of the sacrum and exits through the greater sciatic foramen to insert onto the greater trochanter, serving as the key landmark of the gluteal and deep pelvic regions.

open.q: Which muscle exits the pelvis via the greater sciatic foramen to insert on the greater trochanter of the femur?

questions.q: Which muscle exits the pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen?
questions.explain: The tendon of the obturator internus exits the lesser pelvis through the lesser sciatic foramen, hooking around the lesser sciatic notch to insert on the medial surface of the greater trochanter.

open.q: The tendon of which pelvic wall muscle passes through the lesser sciatic foramen?

questions.q: Which three muscles constitute the levator ani?
options: Bulbocavernosus, ischiocavernosus, and superficial transverse perineal
questions.explain: The levator ani consists of three paired muscular components: puborectalis, pubococcygeus, and iliococcygeus. Together with the coccygeus (ischiococcygeus) posteriorly, they form the pelvic diaphragm.

open.q: Name the three muscular components that make up the levator ani.

questions.q: Which component of the levator ani forms a U-shaped muscular sling around the anorectal junction that maintains the anorectal angle and fecal continence?
questions.explain: The puborectalis arises from the posterior aspect of the body of the pubis and loops posteriorly around the anorectal junction without attaching to the coccyx, creating the ~90-degree anorectal angle essential for fecal continence.

open.q: Which part of the levator ani forms a U-shaped sling behind the anorectal junction to maintain fecal continence?

questions.q: From which thickening of the obturator internus fascia does the levator ani arise laterally?
questions.explain: The tendinous arch of the levator ani is a linear thickening of the obturator fascia extending from the body of the pubis to the ischial spine, providing lateral origin for the pubococcygeus and iliococcygeus.

open.q: What is the name of the linear thickening of the obturator fascia that gives lateral origin to the levator ani?

questions.q: Which nerve innervates the pelvic surface of the levator ani?
options: Nerve to levator ani (S3–S4), with pudendal branches inferiorly
questions.explain: The levator ani is innervated superiorly (pelvic surface) by the nerve to levator ani (primarily S4, with contributions from S3) and inferiorly (perineal surface) by branches of the pudendal nerve (S2-S4).

open.q: Which sacral spinal nerve segments supply the nerve to levator ani on its pelvic surface?

questions.q: What is the anatomical apex of the urinary bladder connected to the umbilicus?
questions.explain: The apex of the urinary bladder points anteriorly toward the top of the pubic symphysis and is connected to the umbilicus by the median umbilical ligament (remnant of the urachus).

open.q: Which fibrous ligament extends from the apex of the urinary bladder to the umbilicus?

questions.q: What are the three angles of the trigone of the urinary bladder?
options: Two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice
Two ureteric orifices and the apex of the bladder
The internal urethral orifice, external urethral orifice, and urachus
Two ejaculatory duct openings and the prostatic utricle
questions.explain: The trigone on the internal posterior wall (base/fundus) of the bladder is bounded superolaterally by the right and left ureteric orifices (connected by the interureteric crest) and inferiorly by the internal urethral orifice.

open.q: Name the three openings that form the corners of the trigone on the internal posterior wall of the urinary bladder.
accept: right and left ureteric orifices and internal urethral orifice
two ureteric orifices and internal urethral orifice

questions.q: Which autonomic nerves mediate contraction of the detrusor muscle and relaxation of the internal urethral sphincter during micturition?
questions.explain: Parasympathetic fibers via the pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) stimulate detrusor contraction and inhibit the internal urethral sphincter to empty the bladder. Sympathetic fibers (T11-L2) promote urine storage.

open.q: Which nerves carry the parasympathetic fibers (S2-S4) responsible for contracting the detrusor muscle during micturition?

questions.q: At which vertebral level does the sigmoid colon become the rectum?
questions.explain: The rectosigmoid junction occurs anterior to the third sacral vertebra (S3), where the sigmoid mesocolon ends and the teniae coli spread out to form a continuous longitudinal muscle coat.

open.q: Anterior to which sacral vertebra does the sigmoid colon transition into the rectum?

questions.q: Which transverse rectal fold (valve of Houston) is the largest, most constant, and located on the right wall just above the rectal ampulla?
questions.explain: The middle transverse rectal fold (Kohlrausch fold) lies on the right lateral wall about 6 to 8 cm above the anus, corresponding roughly to the level of the peritoneal reflection (rectouterine or rectovesical pouch).

open.q: Which of the three transverse rectal folds (valves of Houston) is the most constant and projects from the right wall of the rectum?

questions.q: Which zone of the prostate gland is the most common site of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)?
questions.explain: Benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) arises predominantly in the periurethral transition zone (causing early urinary obstruction), whereas prostate adenocarcinoma arises most often in the posterior peripheral zone (palpable on digital rectal exam).

open.q: Which anatomical zone of the prostate gland is the primary site of origin for benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)?

questions.q: Which structures open onto the seminal colliculus (verumontanum) on the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra?
options: Bulbourethral gland ducts and ureteric orifices
Ductus deferens and seminal vesicle ducts separately
questions.explain: The prostatic utricle (embryological remnant of the paramesonephric ducts) opens in the midline of the seminal colliculus, flanked on either side by the openings of the right and left ejaculatory ducts.

open.q: Name the three openings located on the seminal colliculus on the posterior wall of the prostatic urethra.
accept: prostatic utricle and two ejaculatory ducts

questions.q: Which structure joins the duct of the seminal vesicle to form the ejaculatory duct?
questions.explain: Each ejaculatory duct is formed posterior to the bladder neck by the union of the duct of the seminal vesicle and the terminal ampulla of the ductus (vas) deferens, then traverses the prostate to enter the prostatic urethra.

open.q: Which two ducts unite posterior to the neck of the urinary bladder to form each ejaculatory duct?
accept: ductus deferens and duct of seminal vesicle
vas deferens and seminal vesicle duct

questions.q: What is the relationship of the ductus deferens to the ureter near the posterolateral angle of the urinary bladder?
options: The ductus deferens crosses superior (anterior) to the ureter
The ureter crosses superior to the ductus deferens
The ductus deferens passes posterior to the seminal vesicle and inferior to the ureter
questions.explain: Just before reaching the fundus of the bladder, the ductus deferens hooks superiorly and anteriorly over the terminal ureter (mnemonic: water under the bridge).

open.q: Near the base of the male urinary bladder, does the ductus deferens pass superior or inferior to the terminal ureter?

questions.q: Which fascial septum separates the posterior surface of the prostate and seminal vesicles from the anterior wall of the rectum?
questions.explain: The rectoprostatic fascia (fascia of Denonvilliers) is a tough, fused peritoneal remnant separating the rectum posteriorly from the prostate, seminal vesicles, and bladder base anteriorly.

open.q: Name the fascial layer separating the rectum posteriorly from the prostate and seminal vesicles anteriorly.

questions.q: What is the normal position of the adult nulliparous uterus relative to the vagina and the uterine cervix?
questions.explain: Normally, the uterus is anteverted (the long axis of the cervix is tilted anteriorly ~90 degrees relative to the axis of the vagina) and anteflexed (the body of the uterus is bent anteriorly ~170 degrees on the cervix).

open.q: State the two anatomical terms describing the normal anterior angulation of the uterus relative to the vagina and cervix.

questions.q: Which ligament of the uterus passes through the inguinal canal to insert into the subcutaneous tissue of the labium majus?
questions.explain: The round ligament of the uterus (derived from the inferior gubernaculum) extends from the uterine horn, passes through the deep inguinal ring and inguinal canal, and terminates in the labium majus.

open.q: Which uterine ligament traverses the inguinal canal to terminate in the labium majus?

questions.q: Which ligament provides the primary passive ligamentous support preventing downward uterine prolapse and transmits the uterine vessels?
questions.explain: The cardinal (transverse cervical or Mackenrodt) ligaments are dense condensations of endopelvic fascia extending from the cervix and lateral vaginal fornices to the lateral pelvic walls, enclosing the uterine arteries and veins.

open.q: Name the condensation of endopelvic fascia extending from the cervix to the lateral pelvic wall that provides primary support against uterine prolapse.

questions.q: During a hysterectomy, ligation of the uterine artery near the lateral vaginal fornix places which structure at greatest risk of iatrogenic injury because it passes directly inferior to the artery?
questions.explain: About 1.5 to 2 cm lateral to the uterine cervix, the uterine artery crosses superior and anterior to the ureter ('water under the bridge'), making the ureter vulnerable during uterine artery clamping.

open.q: Which tubular structure passes directly inferior to the uterine artery approximately 1.5 to 2 cm lateral to the cervix?

questions.q: Which subdivision of the broad ligament suspends the ovary from its posterior layer?
questions.explain: The broad ligament is subdivided into the mesometrium (largest part, attached to the uterus), the mesosalpinx (supporting the uterine tube), and the mesovarium (attaching the ovary to the posterior leaf of the broad ligament).

open.q: Name the portion of the broad ligament that attaches the ovary to the posterior aspect of the broad ligament.

questions.q: Which vessels travel within the suspensory ligament of the ovary (infundibulopelvic ligament)?
questions.explain: The suspensory ligament of the ovary extends superolaterally from the ovary to the lateral pelvic wall and conveys the ovarian vessels, lymphatics, and autonomic nerves.

open.q: Which blood vessels run within the suspensory (infundibulopelvic) ligament of the ovary?

questions.q: Which vaginal fornix is the deepest and lies immediately anterior to the rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas)?
questions.explain: Because the posterior vaginal wall is longer than the anterior wall, the posterior vaginal fornix is the deepest recess and is separated from the rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) only by the vaginal wall and peritoneum—allowing culdocentesis.

open.q: Which vaginal fornix is separated from the rectouterine pouch (pouch of Douglas) only by the vaginal wall and peritoneum?

questions.q: In which segment of the uterine (fallopian) tube does fertilization normally occur?
questions.explain: The ampulla is the widest and longest section of the uterine tube and is the usual site of fertilization.

open.q: In which part of the uterine tube does fertilization typically take place?

questions.q: Where does lymph from the ovaries and fundus of the uterus primarily drain?
questions.explain: Lymphatics from the ovary, uterine tube, and fundus of the uterus follow the ovarian vessels superiorly to the lumbar (para-aortic / lateral aortic) lymph nodes at the L1-L2 level.

open.q: To which group of abdominal lymph nodes does lymph from the ovaries and uterine fundus primarily drain?

questions.q: Which lymph nodes receive lymph from the lower third of the vagina (below the hymen) and the labia majora?
questions.explain: Lymph from the perineum, vulva, and lower vagina (inferior to the hymen) drains to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes, whereas the upper vagina and cervix drain to the internal and external iliac nodes.

open.q: To which lymph nodes does lymph from the lower third of the vagina (below the hymen) drain?

questions.q: Which artery is typically the largest branch of the posterior division of the internal iliac artery?
questions.explain: The posterior division of the internal iliac artery gives off three branches: the iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal arteries—with the superior gluteal artery being the largest branch, passing between the lumbosacral trunk and S1 ventral ramus.

open.q: Name the three branches arising from the posterior division of the internal iliac artery.
accept: iliolumbar, lateral sacral, and superior gluteal arteries

questions.q: Which branch of the internal iliac artery is frequently absent in males (replaced by the inferior vesical artery) and arises from the anterior division in females?
questions.explain: The vaginal artery in females is homologous to the inferior vesical artery in males and arises from the anterior division of the internal iliac artery (or from the uterine artery).

open.q: Which branch of the anterior division of the internal iliac artery in females is the anatomical homologue of the male inferior vesical artery?

questions.q: Which branch of the internal iliac artery may arise aberrantly from the inferior epigastric artery ('corona mortis') and cross the superior pubic ramus?
questions.explain: An aberrant (accessory or replaced) obturator artery arises from the inferior epigastric artery in ~20-30% of people and descends across the pelvic brim/lacunar ligament toward the obturator canal, posing a severe bleeding risk during femoral hernia or pelvic surgery.

open.q: An aberrant branch of which pelvic artery arises from the inferior epigastric artery and forms the vascular anastomosis known as the corona mortis?

questions.q: Which spinal nerve roots contribute to the pudendal nerve?
questions.explain: The pudendal nerve arises from the ventral rami of S2, S3, and S4 of the sacral plexus ('S2, 3, 4 keep the pelvic floor off the floor').

open.q: Which sacral spinal nerve roots form the pudendal nerve?

questions.q: Which path does the pudendal nerve take to leave the pelvis and enter the perineum?
options: Greater sciatic foramen → around ischial spine → lesser sciatic foramen
Lesser sciatic foramen → greater sciatic foramen
questions.explain: The pudendal nerve (along with the internal pudendal vessels) leaves the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen below piriformis, crosses posterior to the ischial spine/sacrospinous ligament, and enters the pudendal canal via the lesser sciatic foramen.

open.q: Around which bony landmark does the pudendal nerve hook after exiting the greater sciatic foramen before entering the lesser sciatic foramen?

questions.q: The lumbosacral trunk (L4, L5) descends over the ala of the sacrum to join the sacral plexus. Why can a fetal head compress it during a difficult labor?
options: Crosses the sacral ala at the pelvic brim and may be compressed by the fetal head
Lies anterior to the pubic symphysis
questions.explain: Unlike the sacral ventral rami that rest on the piriformis muscle, the lumbosacral trunk crosses directly over the bare bony ala of the sacrum at the pelvic inlet, making it vulnerable to compression by the fetal head (causing postpartum foot drop).

open.q: Which spinal nerve roots unite to form the lumbosacral trunk that crosses the ala of the sacrum to join the sacral plexus?

questions.q: Which nerves form the superior hypogastric plexus anterior to the bifurcation of the abdominal aorta and body of L5?
options: Lumbar splanchnic nerves and the aortic plexus
questions.explain: The superior hypogastric plexus is a sympathetic plexus formed inferior to the aortic bifurcation by the continuation of the intermesenteric plexus and lumbar splanchnic nerves (L1-L2). It divides into left and right hypogastric nerves.

open.q: Into which two nerves does the superior hypogastric plexus divide as it enters the lesser pelvis?

questions.q: In the male pelvic autonomic system, which nerve fibers mediate emission (contraction of ductus deferens, seminal vesicles, and prostate) versus erection?
options: Sympathetic fibres mediate emission; parasympathetic fibres mediate erection
Parasympathetic fibres mediate emission; sympathetic fibres mediate erection
questions.explain: Parasympathetic pelvic splanchnic nerves (S2-S4) cause vasodilation of helicine arteries for erection ('Point'), sympathetic hypogastric nerves (T11-L2) cause smooth muscle contraction for emission ('Shoot'), and somatic pudendal nerve branches cause bulbospongiosus contraction for ejaculation.

open.q: Distinguish the autonomic divisions responsible for penile erection versus seminal emission.
accept: parasympathetic mediates erection and sympathetic mediates emission
erection is parasympathetic, emission is sympathetic

questions.q: What are the boundaries of the diamond-shaped perineum when viewed from below in the lithotomy position?
options: Pubic symphysis anteriorly, coccyx posteriorly, and ischial tuberosities laterally
Sacral promontory posteriorly, pubic crest anteriorly, and iliac crests laterally
Inguinal ligaments anteriorly, coccyx posteriorly, and greater trochanters laterally
Ischial spines laterally, pubic symphysis anteriorly, and sacrum posteriorly
questions.explain: The perineum corresponds to the pelvic outlet, bounded anteriorly by the pubic symphysis, anterolaterally by the ischiopubic rami, laterally by the ischial tuberosities, posterolaterally by the sacrotuberous ligaments, and posteriorly by the tip of the coccyx.

open.q: Name the anterior, posterior, and lateral bony landmarks that define the diamond-shaped boundaries of the perineum.
accept: pubic symphysis, coccyx, and ischial tuberosities
pubic symphysis anteriorly, coccyx posteriorly, ischial tuberosities laterally

questions.q: An imaginary transverse line connecting which two landmarks divides the perineum into an anterior urogenital triangle and a posterior anal triangle?
questions.explain: A transverse line joining the anterior ends of the two ischial tuberosities divides the perineum into the anterior urogenital triangle and posterior anal triangle, with the perineal body located at its midpoint.

open.q: Between which two bony landmarks is the transverse line drawn to divide the perineum into the urogenital and anal triangles?

questions.q: What forms the lateral wall of the ischioanal (ischiorectal) fossa?
options: Obturator internus muscle and obturator fascia
External anal sphincter and levator ani
questions.explain: The wedge-shaped ischioanal fossa is bounded laterally by the ischial tuberosity and obturator internus muscle covered by obturator fascia (containing the pudendal canal), medially by the levator ani and external anal sphincter, and inferiorly by perianal skin.

open.q: Which muscle and its covering fascia form the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa?

questions.q: The pudendal canal (Alcock canal) is a fascial tunnel located on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa within which fascia?
questions.explain: The pudendal canal (Alcock canal) is formed by a splitting of the obturator fascia along the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa and transmits the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal artery and veins.

open.q: Within which fascial layer on the lateral wall of the ischioanal fossa is the pudendal canal (Alcock canal) formed?

questions.q: How can a unilateral ischioanal abscess spread across the midline to form a 'horseshoe abscess'?
options: Posterior to the anal canal through the deep postanal space
Anterior to the urethra through the superficial perineal pouch
Superiorly through the levator ani into the peritoneal cavity
questions.explain: The left and right ischioanal fossae communicate posteriorly behind the anal canal via the deep postanal space (inferior to the levator ani and superior to the anococcygeal ligament), allowing infection to spread from one side to the other.

open.q: Through which anatomical space behind the anal canal do the right and left ischioanal fossae communicate?

questions.q: Which landmark in the anal canal marks the junction between the embryological hindgut (endoderm) and proctodeum (ectoderm)?
questions.explain: The pectinate (dentate) line is formed by the inferior edges of the anal valves and represents the developmental junction between endodermal hindgut above and ectodermal proctodeum below.

open.q: What is the name of the serrated line in the anal canal formed by the anal valves that separates visceral upper from somatic lower anal canal?

questions.q: Why are internal hemorrhoids above the pectinate line painless, whereas external hemorrhoids below the pectinate line are exquisitely painful?
options: Above: visceral afferents predominate; below: somatic inferior rectal nerves carry pain
Above: no blood supply; below: dense arterioles
Above: femoral nerve; below: vagus nerve
Above: keratinised skin; below: columnar epithelium
questions.explain: Mucosa superior to the pectinate line receives autonomic visceral innervation (insensitive to cutting/pain, sensitive only to stretch), whereas anoderm inferior to the pectinate line receives somatic sensory innervation from the inferior rectal branches of the pudendal nerve.

open.q: Which nerve supplies somatic sensory innervation to the anal canal inferior to the pectinate line?
accept: inferior rectal branch of pudendal nerve

questions.q: Where does lymph from the anal canal inferior to the pectinate line drain?
questions.explain: Lymph superior to the pectinate line drains to the internal iliac and inferior mesenteric nodes, whereas lymph inferior to the pectinate line drains to the superficial inguinal lymph nodes.

open.q: To which group of lymph nodes does lymph from the anal canal below the pectinate line drain?

questions.q: What are the boundaries of the superficial perineal pouch?
options: Superiorly by the perineal membrane and inferiorly by Colles fascia
Superiorly by the pelvic diaphragm and inferiorly by the perineal membrane
Superiorly by Scarpa fascia and inferiorly by Buck fascia
Superiorly by the obturator membrane and inferiorly by the skin
questions.explain: The superficial perineal pouch lies between the perineal membrane (inferior fascia of the urogenital diaphragm) superiorly and the membranous layer of superficial perineal fascia (Colles fascia) inferiorly.

open.q: Name the superior and inferior fascial boundaries of the superficial perineal pouch.
accept: perineal membrane superiorly and Colles fascia inferiorly

questions.q: A 32-year-old man falls astride a metal bar, rupturing his bulbous (spongy) urethra inferior to the perineal membrane. Into which region will extravasated urine NOT spread due to the attachments of Colles fascia?
options: Medial thigh, below the fascia lata attachment
Lower abdominal wall deep to Scarpa fascia
questions.explain: Colles fascia attaches posteriorly to the posterior border of the perineal membrane and laterally to the ischiopubic rami and fascia lata along the groin crease, preventing urine from entering the thigh or anal triangle while allowing spread into the scrotum, penis, and anterior abdominal wall.

open.q: Why does urine extravasating into the superficial perineal pouch from a bulbous urethral rupture fail to enter the thigh or anal triangle?
accept: Colles fascia attaches to the ischiopubic rami, fascia lata, and posterior border of perineal membrane

questions.q: Which structures are contained within the deep perineal pouch in both sexes?
options: External urethral sphincter, deep transverse perineal muscle and related structures
Vestibular bulbs and greater vestibular glands
questions.explain: The deep perineal pouch lies superior to the perineal membrane and contains the external urethral sphincter, deep transverse perineal muscles, branches of the internal pudendal vessels, dorsal nerves of the penis/clitoris, and (in males) the membranous urethra and bulbourethral (Cowper) glands.

open.q: Which pair of mucus-secreting glands in males is embedded within the external urethral sphincter in the deep perineal pouch?

questions.q: Into which part of the male urethra do the ducts of the bulbourethral (Cowper) glands open?
questions.explain: Although the bulbourethral glands lie in the deep perineal pouch alongside the membranous urethra, their ducts pierce the perineal membrane to open into the proximal (bulbar) part of the spongy urethra.

open.q: Into which segment of the male urethra do the ducts of the bulbourethral glands empty?

questions.q: Which structures are located in the superficial perineal pouch in females?
options: Clitoral crura, vestibular bulbs and greater vestibular glands
Greater vestibular glands and external urethral sphincter
Internal urethral sphincter and levator ani
questions.explain: In females, the superficial perineal pouch contains the crura of the clitoris (covered by ischiocavernosus), the bulbs of the vestibule (covered by bulbospongiosus), the superficial transverse perineal muscles, and the greater vestibular (Bartholin) glands.

open.q: Which mucus-secreting glands in the female superficial perineal pouch are homologous to the male bulbourethral glands?

questions.q: Which muscle covers the crus of the penis or clitoris and attaches to the ischiopubic ramus?
questions.explain: The ischiocavernosus muscle arises from the ischial tuberosity and ischiopubic ramus and envelops the crus of the penis or clitoris, compressing it to maintain erection.

open.q: Which perineal muscle envelops the crus of the penis or clitoris?

questions.q: What is the arrangement of the dorsal neurovascular structures on the dorsum of the penis deep to Buck fascia from medial to lateral?
options: Deep dorsal vein (midline), dorsal artery, dorsal nerve
Dorsal artery (midline), deep dorsal vein, dorsal nerve
Dorsal nerve (midline), dorsal artery, deep dorsal vein
Superficial dorsal vein, dorsal nerve, dorsal artery
questions.explain: Deep to the deep fascia of the penis (Buck fascia), the single deep dorsal vein sits in the midline between the paired dorsal arteries, with the paired dorsal nerves positioned most laterally (mnemonic: VAN from medial to lateral).

open.q: State the order of the deep dorsal vein, dorsal artery, and dorsal nerve on the dorsum of the penis from medial to lateral.
accept: deep dorsal vein, dorsal artery, dorsal nerve

questions.q: The perineal body (central tendon of the perineum) serves as the fibromuscular convergence point for several muscles. Which muscle does NOT attach to the perineal body?
questions.explain: The perineal body receives attachments from the bulbospongiosus, superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles, external anal sphincter, external urethral sphincter, and fibers of the levator ani. The ischiocavernosus attaches laterally to the ischiopubic ramus.

questions.q: During a mediolateral episiotomy performed to prevent an uncontrolled tear of the perineal body during childbirth, the incision is directed posterolaterally from the posterior fourchette. Which structure is intentionally avoided by angling laterally rather than cutting straight posteriorly?
options: External anal sphincter and anal canal
questions.explain: A mediolateral episiotomy angles 45 to 60 degrees posterolaterally into the lower perineal tissues/bulbospongiosus to prevent extension into the perineal body, external anal sphincter, and rectal mucosa.

open.q: Which sphincter and visceral structure are protected from tearing by angling a mediolateral episiotomy 45 to 60 degrees posterolaterally?
accept: external anal sphincter and anal canal

questions.q: To perform a transvaginal pudendal nerve block during labor, the clinician palpates which bony prominence through the lateral vaginal wall as the needle target?
questions.explain: Because the pudendal nerve hooks directly posterior to the sacrospinous ligament near its attachment to the ischial spine, palpating the ischial spine transvaginally guides accurate local anesthetic infiltration.

open.q: Which bony landmark is palpated transvaginally to guide needle placement for a pudendal nerve block?

questions.q: Which layer of the scrotal wall is continuous with both Scarpa fascia of the abdomen and Colles fascia of the perineum and contains smooth muscle?
questions.explain: The dartos fascia (tunic) is fat-free superficial fascia containing smooth muscle fibers (dartos muscle) that wrinkle scrotal skin in cold temperatures; it is directly continuous with Scarpa and Colles fasciae.

open.q: Name the smooth-muscle-containing subcutaneous layer of the scrotum that is continuous with Scarpa and Colles fasciae.

questions.q: A clinical fluid collection (hydrocele) within the scrotum accumulates between the parietal and visceral layers of which serous membrane?
questions.explain: The tunica vaginalis is a closed peritoneal sac derived from the distal processus vaginalis covering the anterior and lateral surfaces of the testis; excess serous fluid between its parietal and visceral layers forms a hydrocele.

open.q: Between the parietal and visceral layers of which serous membrane does fluid accumulate in a scrotal hydrocele?

questions.q: Where do lymphatics from the testis (parenchyma) drain, in contrast to lymphatics from the scrotal skin?
options: Testis: lumbar nodes; scrotal skin: superficial inguinal nodes
questions.explain: Because the testes descend from the posterior abdominal wall, their lymphatic drainage ascends with the testicular vessels to the lumbar (para-aortic) lymph nodes, whereas scrotal skin drains to the superficial inguinal nodes.

open.q: Contrast the primary lymph node drainage of the testis with that of the scrotal wall.
accept: testis drains to lumbar (para-aortic) nodes and scrotum drains to superficial inguinal nodes
testis to para-aortic nodes, scrotum to superficial inguinal nodes

questions.q: Which segment of the male urethra is the shortest, narrowest (except for the external meatus), and most fixed as it traverses the deep perineal pouch?
questions.explain: The membranous urethra (about 1 to 1.5 cm long) passes through the deep perineal pouch surrounded by the external urethral sphincter; it is fixed by the perineal membrane and is the most susceptible segment to shearing injury in pelvic fractures.

open.q: Which segment of the male urethra traverses the external urethral sphincter and is most prone to rupture in pelvic fractures?

questions.q: A clinician documents the location of an abdominal mass using the four-quadrant system. Which two planes divide the abdomen into right upper, left upper, right lower and left lower quadrants?
questions.explain: The four abdominal quadrants are formed by the median (midsagittal) plane and the transumbilical plane, which intersect at the umbilicus. The nine-region scheme instead uses two midclavicular planes and the subcostal and transtubercular planes.

open.q: Which two planes are used to divide the abdomen into four clinical quadrants?

questions.q: A patient sustains a superficial laceration of the anterior scrotal skin. Which pair of nerves provides most of its anterior cutaneous innervation?
options: Ilioinguinal nerve and genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve
Pudendal nerve and posterior femoral cutaneous nerve
Iliohypogastric nerve and lateral femoral cutaneous nerve
questions.explain: The anterior scrotal nerves arise mainly from the ilioinguinal nerve and the genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve. Posterior scrotal branches are supplied by the perineal branch of the pudendal nerve and the posterior femoral cutaneous nerve.

open.q: Which two nerves supply most of the anterior scrotal skin?
accept: ilioinguinal and genital branch of genitofemoral
ilioinguinal nerve and genital branch of genitofemoral nerve

questions.q: The pampiniform venous plexus surrounds the testicular artery within the spermatic cord. What is its principal contribution to testicular temperature regulation?
options: It produces heat through smooth-muscle contraction
It cools arterial blood by countercurrent heat exchange
It prevents lymphatic drainage from the testis
It increases arterial pressure within the testicular artery
questions.explain: The pampiniform plexus forms a countercurrent heat exchanger around the testicular artery. Cooler venous blood returning from the testis removes heat from incoming arterial blood, helping maintain the lower temperature required for normal spermatogenesis.

open.q: How does the pampiniform plexus help maintain testicular temperature?
accept: cools arterial blood by countercurrent exchange
countercurrent cooling of testicular arterial blood

questions.q: Histological examination of the suprarenal medulla reveals chromaffin cells. From which embryological cell population are these cells derived?
questions.explain: The suprarenal medulla develops from neural crest cells that migrate into the developing gland and differentiate into chromaffin cells. The suprarenal cortex, in contrast, is derived from mesoderm.

open.q: What is the embryological origin of the chromaffin cells of the suprarenal medulla?

questions.q: A renal calculus obstructs the outlet of a minor renal calyx. Which structure normally receives urine directly from the renal papilla before it reaches the major calyces?
questions.explain: The renal papilla projects into a minor calyx, which receives urine from the papillary ducts. Minor calyces unite to form major calyces, which drain into the renal pelvis and then the ureter.

open.q: Into which structure does a renal papilla project and empty?

questions.q: During posterior abdominal wall dissection, a thickened arch of fascia is identified passing over quadratus lumborum and giving attachment to the diaphragm. Which structure is this?
questions.explain: The lateral arcuate ligament is a thickening of the fascia covering quadratus lumborum. The medial arcuate ligament arches over psoas major, while the median arcuate ligament joins the right and left crura over the aorta.

open.q: Which arcuate ligament arches over quadratus lumborum?

questions.q: During laparoscopic appendicectomy, the appendix is difficult to locate because its tip is displaced behind the caecum. Which feature reliably helps the surgeon identify the base of the appendix?
options: Convergence of the three taeniae coli
The appendicular artery entering the tip
questions.explain: The three taeniae coli converge at the base of the vermiform appendix and provide a reliable guide to locating it. The tip is variable in position; a retrocaecal position is common.

open.q: What anatomical feature reliably identifies the base of the vermiform appendix?
accept: convergence of the three taeniae coli

questions.q: A newborn is diagnosed with intestinal malrotation. During normal development, through how many degrees does the midgut rotate around the superior mesenteric artery, viewed from the front?
questions.explain: The midgut normally undergoes a total 270-degree counterclockwise rotation around the axis of the superior mesenteric artery when viewed anteriorly. This occurs in stages as the midgut herniates physiologically and returns to the abdominal cavity.

open.q: How many degrees and in which direction does the midgut rotate around the superior mesenteric artery when viewed anteriorly?
accept: two hundred and seventy degrees counterclockwise

questions.sub: Liver, Biliary Tract, Pancreas, and Spleen
questions.q: A surgeon controls hepatic inflow by clamping the hepatoduodenal ligament. Which three structures make up the portal triad within this ligament?
options: Portal vein, proper hepatic artery and common bile duct
Inferior vena cava, hepatic veins and cystic duct
Hepatic artery, hepatic veins and pancreatic duct
Portal vein, splenic artery and common hepatic duct
questions.explain: The portal triad consists of the portal vein, proper hepatic artery and bile duct (typically the common bile duct in the free edge of the hepatoduodenal ligament). The portal vein lies posteriorly; the bile duct is to the right and the proper hepatic artery to the left.

open.q: Name the three structures of the portal triad in the hepatoduodenal ligament.
accept: portal vein, proper hepatic artery and bile duct
portal vein proper hepatic artery common bile duct

questions.sub: Liver, Biliary Tract, Pancreas, and Spleen
questions.q: A gallstone becomes lodged at the neck of the gallbladder. Which mucosal feature of the cystic duct helps maintain its patency and permits bile to flow in either direction?
questions.explain: The mucosa of the neck of the gallbladder and cystic duct forms spiral folds, often called the spiral valve. These folds help keep the cystic duct open and allow bile to enter or leave the gallbladder.

open.q: What are the spiral mucosal folds in the cystic duct commonly called?

questions.sub: Liver, Biliary Tract, Pancreas, and Spleen
questions.q: A portal vein is being identified during pancreatic surgery. At which location is it usually formed by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins?
options: Anterior to the neck of the pancreas
Posterior to the neck of the pancreas
Within the hepatoduodenal ligament at the porta hepatis
At the inferior border of the spleen
questions.explain: The portal vein is usually formed posterior to the neck of the pancreas by the union of the superior mesenteric vein and splenic vein. It then ascends within the hepatoduodenal ligament toward the porta hepatis.

open.q: Where is the portal vein usually formed by the union of the superior mesenteric and splenic veins?
accept: posterior to the neck of the pancreas
behind the neck of the pancreas

questions.q: A student describes the boundaries of the pelvic cavity during an oral examination. Which statement correctly identifies its superior and inferior limits?
options: The pelvic inlet is superior and the pelvic outlet is inferior
The pelvic outlet is superior and the pelvic inlet is inferior
The pelvic diaphragm forms the superior boundary and the sacral promontory forms the inferior boundary
The obturator membrane forms both the superior and inferior boundaries
questions.explain: The pelvic inlet forms the superior opening of the pelvic cavity and the pelvic outlet forms its inferior opening. The pelvic diaphragm closes the outlet, separating the pelvic cavity from the perineum.

open.q: What are the superior and inferior openings of the pelvic cavity called?

questions.q: During examination of a dry hip bone, a student identifies the concavity between the ischial spine and ischial tuberosity. Which anatomical feature is this?
questions.explain: The lesser sciatic notch lies between the ischial spine and ischial tuberosity. With the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments, it contributes to the lesser sciatic foramen.

open.q: What is the notch between the ischial spine and ischial tuberosity called?

questions.q: A pelvic operation places the superior gluteal nerve at risk as it leaves the pelvis. Through which route does this nerve enter the gluteal region?
options: Greater sciatic foramen superior to piriformis
Greater sciatic foramen inferior to piriformis
questions.explain: The superior gluteal nerve exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen superior to piriformis. Most other major nerves entering the gluteal region, including the sciatic and inferior gluteal nerves, pass inferior to piriformis.

open.q: Where does the superior gluteal nerve pass in relation to piriformis as it exits the pelvis?
accept: through the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis

questions.q: During dissection of the posterior pelvic wall, a chain of sympathetic ganglia is identified on each side of the sacrum. Approximately how many ganglia are usually present in each sacral sympathetic trunk?
questions.explain: Each sacral sympathetic trunk usually contains four small ganglia, although the exact number can vary. The two trunks descend on the pelvic surface of the sacrum and unite inferiorly at the ganglion impar.

open.q: How many ganglia are usually present in each sacral sympathetic trunk?

questions.q: During endoscopic examination of the prostatic urethra, the clinician identifies the paired grooves on either side of the urethral crest. Which structures normally open into these grooves?
questions.explain: The prostatic sinuses are grooves on either side of the urethral crest and receive the openings of the prostatic ductules. The ejaculatory ducts open into the prostatic urethra near the seminal colliculus.

open.q: Which ducts open into the prostatic sinuses?

questions.q: A clinician examines the external urethral opening in a woman and identifies two small paraurethral duct openings nearby. Where do the paraurethral glands normally drain?
questions.explain: The paraurethral (Skene) glands are located near the distal urethra. Their ducts open on either side of the external urethral orifice; they are homologous to the prostate in males.

open.q: Where do the ducts of the female paraurethral glands open?
accept: on either side of the urethral opening

questions.q: During a vasectomy, the surgeon isolates the ductus deferens within the spermatic cord. From which part of the epididymis does this duct begin?
questions.explain: The ductus deferens begins as the continuation of the tail of the epididymis. It ascends in the spermatic cord, passes through the inguinal canal and enters the pelvis.

open.q: From which part of the epididymis does the ductus deferens begin?

questions.q: A lesion damages the pelvic splanchnic nerves bilaterally. Which spinal nerve roots give rise to these nerves?
questions.explain: The pelvic splanchnic nerves arise from the anterior rami of S2–S4 and carry preganglionic parasympathetic fibres to pelvic plexuses and hindgut structures. They are distinct from the sympathetic sacral splanchnic nerves.

open.q: Which sacral spinal nerve roots give rise to the pelvic splanchnic nerves?

questions.q: A stone becomes impacted where the ureter crosses the pelvic brim. Which vessel does it normally cross at this site?
options: Bifurcation of the common iliac artery or the beginning of the external iliac artery
questions.explain: The ureter crosses the iliac vessels at the pelvic brim, commonly at the bifurcation of the common iliac artery or over the beginning of the external iliac artery.

open.q: Name the structure or anatomical relationship tested in this clinical scenario.
accept: bifurcation of the common iliac artery or the beginning of the external iliac artery

questions.q: A surgeon ligates the artery supplying the midgut during resection of an ischaemic bowel segment. Which artery is being ligated?
questions.explain: The superior mesenteric artery supplies the midgut, from the distal duodenum through the proximal two-thirds of the transverse colon.

open.q: Name the structure or anatomical relationship tested in this clinical scenario.

questions.q: A direct inguinal hernia protrudes through a weakened posterior wall of the inguinal canal. Relative to the inferior epigastric vessels, where does it emerge?
questions.explain: A direct inguinal hernia passes through Hesselbach's triangle, medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. An indirect hernia enters the deep ring lateral to these vessels.

open.q: Name the structure or anatomical relationship tested in this clinical scenario.

questions.q: During hysterectomy, the uterine artery is ligated close to the cervix. Which structure is at risk because it passes inferior to the uterine artery?
questions.explain: The ureter passes beneath the uterine artery near the cervix ('water under the bridge'), making it vulnerable during uterine artery ligation.

open.q: Name the structure or anatomical relationship tested in this clinical scenario.

questions.q: A patient has an injury to the pudendal nerve near the ischial spine. Which route does the nerve normally take to enter the perineum?
options: It exits the pelvis through the greater sciatic foramen and re-enters through the lesser sciatic foramen
